noteBlocks.lede: You cannot see photosynthesis happening, so you test for the starch it leaves behind. Destarch the plant first, take away one thing — light, carbon dioxide or chlorophyll — and the pattern of blue-black on the leaf afterwards tells you what the plant needed.

noteBlocks.md: Boil a leaf, take the green out with ethanol and drop iodine on it: where the leaf made starch it turns blue-black. That one colour change is how you prove a plant needs light, carbon dioxide and chlorophyll. Every step in the method has a reason.

noteBlocks.md:
**Why each step happens.**
**1 Boil in water** — kills the leaf, stops its reactions and breaks the cells open so the next liquids can get in.
**2 Boil in ethanol, in a water bath** — the chlorophyll dissolves out, so the green colour cannot hide the result. Ethanol catches fire easily, so **the Bunsen is turned off** and the tube stands in hot water.
**3 Dip in hot water** — the ethanol leaves the leaf brittle; the water softens it so it can be spread flat.
**4 Iodine solution on a white tile** — the white background is what lets you see the blue-black.

noteBlocks.prompt: Why is the Bunsen turned off before the leaf goes into the ethanol?
options: ethanol would turn the leaf blue
noteBlocks.explain: Ethanol is flammable, so it is heated in a water bath with the flame out.

Examiners reported that many candidates gave a general rule — tie your hair back, wear goggles — and got nothing, because the precaution has to match the hazard in front of it. Ethanol is flammable, so the answer is about the flame.

options: To remove the chlorophyll so the colour change can be seen
noteBlocks.answer: To remove the chlorophyll so the colour change can be seen
noteBlocks.explain: Killing is step 1 and softening is step 3. Ethanol is there to take the green out.

noteBlocks.md: **Destarching comes first.** Leave the plant in the **dark for 48 hours**. The leaves use up the starch they already had, so any starch you find afterwards must have been made during the investigation. Skip this and the result proves nothing — every leaf would go blue-black whatever you did to it.

noteBlocks.prompt: To destarch a plant you leave it in the dark for about how many hours?
noteBlocks.explain: Forty-eight hours — two days. The mark for 'why' is that the starch already in the leaves is used up.

noteBlocks.md:
**Light** — clip black card over part of one leaf and leave the plant in the light for 48 hours. The covered strip stays yellow-brown, the rest goes blue-black.
**Carbon dioxide** — seal a leaf in a flask standing over **sodium hydroxide solution**, which absorbs the carbon dioxide. That leaf stays yellow-brown even in full light.
**Chlorophyll** — use a **variegated** leaf, one with green and white parts. Only the green parts go blue-black.

noteBlocks.credit: Forest and Kim Starr, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0
noteBlocks.caption: A variegated geranium: dark green in the middle, cream-white round the edge.
noteBlocks.prompt: This leaf is destarched, left in bright light for 48 hours and tested for starch. Sketch which parts go blue-black, and say what that shows.
A destarched variegated leaf is left in bright light and tested for starch. Which parts turn blue-black?
noteBlocks.explain: The white parts have no chlorophyll, so they cannot absorb light energy and make no starch. That is the whole point of using a variegated leaf.

noteBlocks.title: Why a variegated leaf beats two separate plants
noteBlocks.md: Two plants would differ in more than their chlorophyll — age, water, how much light each one caught. On one variegated leaf the green and white parts share the same temperature, the same light, the same water and the same carbon dioxide. **Only the chlorophyll is different**, so only the chlorophyll can explain the difference in result. That is what makes the investigation valid.

noteBlocks.alt: Three slices of apple on a bench after iodine solution has been added: the first has stained blue-black only in a ring near the skin, the second is blue-black over most of its area with a pale centre, and the third is blue-black almost all over
noteBlocks.caption: Iodine solution on cut slices: where there is starch the tissue stains blue-black; where there is little or none it stays pale.
noteBlocks.prompt: One slice is blue-black only near its edge. What does the pale centre tell you, and what would you have to do before you could say the same about a leaf?

noteBlocks.md: **Oxygen is the other half of the equation.** Pondweed in water under a lamp gives off bubbles; collect them in an inverted test tube and test the gas with a **glowing splint**. If the splint **relights**, the gas is oxygen. Counting the bubbles per minute is how the same apparatus turns into a rate investigation.

noteBlocks.prompt: How do you show the gas collected from pondweed is oxygen?
options: A lit splint gives a squeaky pop
noteBlocks.explain: The squeaky pop is hydrogen and milky limewater is carbon dioxide. Oxygen relights a glowing splint.

noteBlocks.md: A conclusion is only as good as its comparison. 'The covered part had no starch' proves nothing by itself; **'the covered part had no starch while the uncovered part of the same leaf did'** proves that light is needed. Write both halves. The same rule applies to the flask and to the variegated leaf.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which sentence would earn the conclusion mark?
options: The covered part stayed yellow-brown but the uncovered part of the same leaf went blue-black, so light is needed
The leaf went blue-black, so photosynthesis happened
There was no starch in the leaf because there was no light
noteBlocks.answer: The covered part stayed yellow-brown but the uncovered part of the same leaf went blue-black, so light is needed
noteBlocks.explain: It names both parts, both colours and the conclusion. The other two either leave out the comparison or restate the question.

items.stem: Why is a plant destarched before the investigation?
items.skill: Give the reason for destarching, not just the method

options.text: So that any starch already in the leaves is used up
options.feedback: Then any starch found afterwards must have been made during the investigation. Method: 48 hours in the dark.

options.text: So that the leaves lose their chlorophyll
options.feedback: Chlorophyll is removed later, by the ethanol. Destarching is about the starch store, not the green colour.

options.text: So that the leaves take in more carbon dioxide
options.feedback: Darkness does not change how much carbon dioxide a leaf takes in. It stops photosynthesis so the stored starch is used up.

options.text: So that the leaves are soft enough to test
options.feedback: Softening happens in step 3 of the starch test, in hot water. Destarching happens days earlier.

items.stem: The leaf is put into a test tube of ethanol. Why is the Bunsen burner turned off first?
items.skill: Match a safety precaution to the hazard in front of you

options.text: Ethanol is flammable and would catch fire
options.feedback: That is the hazard, so that is the precaution. The tube stands in a beaker of hot water instead.

options.text: The leaf would be burnt
options.feedback: The leaf is already dead by this point; the danger is the ethanol vapour. Name the substance and why it is dangerous.

options.text: Because you should always tie your hair back
options.feedback: A general laboratory rule earns nothing. Summer 2024 examiners reported this exact answer being given instead of the flame. Match the precaution to the hazard.

options.text: The ethanol would evaporate too quickly
options.feedback: It does evaporate, but the reason for the precaution is the fire risk, not the loss of liquid.

items.stem: Which solution is used to absorb carbon dioxide inside a sealed flask?
items.skill: Name the reagent that removes carbon dioxide

options.text: sodium hydroxide solution
options.feedback: Sodium hydroxide absorbs carbon dioxide, so the leaf in that flask cannot photosynthesise.

options.text: iodine solution
options.feedback: Iodine is the test for starch at the end. It does nothing to carbon dioxide.

options.text: sodium hydrogencarbonate solution
options.feedback: That releases carbon dioxide — it is what you add to give pondweed more. The one that takes carbon dioxide away is sodium hydroxide.

options.text: ethanol
options.feedback: Ethanol removes chlorophyll from a leaf that has already been boiled. It is not in the flask.

items.stem: A destarched variegated leaf is left in bright light for 48 hours and then tested for starch. What is seen?

options.text: The green parts turn blue-black; the white parts stay yellow-brown
options.feedback: Only the green parts have chlorophyll, so only they can absorb light energy and make starch.

options.text: The white parts turn blue-black; the green parts stay yellow-brown
options.feedback: It is the other way round. Chlorophyll is what absorbs the light, and the chlorophyll is in the green tissue.

options.text: The whole leaf turns blue-black
options.feedback: Then the leaf would show nothing about chlorophyll. The white parts cannot photosynthesise, so they make no starch.

options.text: The whole leaf stays yellow-brown
options.feedback: The green parts had light, carbon dioxide and chlorophyll, so they did photosynthesise and did make starch.

items.stem: In the starch test, what is the water in step 1 for?
items.skill: Match each step of the starch test to its reason

options.text: Boiling water kills the leaf and breaks the cells open
options.feedback: Dead cells with broken membranes let the ethanol and then the iodine reach the starch inside.

options.text: It removes the chlorophyll
options.feedback: That is the ethanol, in step 2. Water does not dissolve chlorophyll.

options.text: It softens the brittle leaf
options.feedback: Softening is step 3, after the ethanol has made the leaf brittle. Step 1 comes before any ethanol.

options.text: It washes off the iodine
options.feedback: The iodine is added last, on a white tile, and is not washed off at all.

accept: otherwise every leaf would test positive whatever the treatment

context.setting: A destarched leaf sealed in a flask over a colourless solution

parts.stem: Name the solution placed in the flask to absorb carbon dioxide.

scheme.for: sodium hydroxide (solution)

commonErrors.feedback: Sodium hydrogencarbonate releases carbon dioxide; it is what you add to give a plant more. The absorber is sodium hydroxide.

parts.stem:
The leaf in the flask is left in bright light for 48 hours and then tested for starch.
Give the colour of the leaf after iodine solution is added, and explain your answer.

accepted: yellow-brown, because with no carbon dioxide the leaf could not photosynthesise and so made no starch

scheme.for: yellow-brown / no colour change
the sodium hydroxide absorbed the carbon dioxide
so photosynthesis could not happen and no starch was made

hints: The leaf had light and chlorophyll, so name the one thing it did not have.
Give the colour first — it is a separate marking point from the explanation.
parts.workedSolution: It stays yellow-brown. The sodium hydroxide absorbed the carbon dioxide inside the flask, so the leaf had no carbon dioxide, could not photosynthesise and made no starch.

commonErrors.feedback: Blue-black means starch is present, and this leaf could not make any. Work from the equation: no carbon dioxide, no glucose, no starch.

figures.prompt: Which parts of this leaf would turn blue-black after 48 hours in bright light?

parts.stem: Explain why only part of a destarched variegated leaf turns blue-black after 48 hours in bright light.

accepted: only the green parts contain chlorophyll so only they can absorb light energy and photosynthesise to make starch

scheme.for: only the green parts turn blue-black / the white parts stay yellow-brown
the green parts contain chlorophyll and the white parts do not
chlorophyll absorbs the light energy, so only the green parts photosynthesise and make starch

hints: Three marks: which parts, what they contain, and what that lets them do.
parts.workedSolution: Only the green parts turn blue-black. The green parts contain chlorophyll and the white parts do not, and chlorophyll is what absorbs the light energy for photosynthesis, so only the green parts made glucose and stored it as starch.

commonErrors.feedback: The green parts are the ones with chlorophyll, so they are the ones that make starch.

parts.stem: Suggest why using one variegated leaf is better than comparing a green plant with a white one.

accepted: the two parts share the same light, temperature, water and carbon dioxide so only the chlorophyll differs

scheme.for: both parts have the same light intensity, temperature, water and carbon dioxide
so chlorophyll is the only variable that differs / it is a fair test
accept: any difference must be due to the chlorophyll

hints: Think about what else would be different if you used two whole plants.
parts.workedSolution: Both parts of the same leaf get the same light, temperature, water and carbon dioxide, so the only thing that differs between them is the chlorophyll. Any difference in the result must therefore be caused by the chlorophyll, which makes the investigation valid.

the splint relights

(white) tile

The leaf is heated in a test tube of ethanol.
Give one safety precaution for this step and a reason for it.

accepted: turn off the Bunsen burner and stand the tube in hot water because ethanol is flammable

scheme.for: turn off the Bunsen burner / use a water bath with no naked flame
because ethanol is flammable / would catch fire
scheme.examinerNote: General laboratory rules unrelated to the hazard score nothing (Summer 2024).

hints: Name the hazard, then the precaution that deals with that hazard.
parts.workedSolution: Turn the Bunsen burner off and stand the test tube in a beaker of hot water, because ethanol is flammable and would catch fire near a naked flame.

commonErrors.feedback: Summer 2024 examiners reported general safety instructions being given here instead of the one that matches the hazard. Ethanol is flammable, so the answer is about the flame.

accepted: whether the part of the leaf is covered; the colour with iodine solution; the time in the light

scheme.for: independent: whether that part of the leaf is covered by foil / whether light reaches it
dependent: the colour of that part with iodine solution / whether starch is present
control: the time in the light / the temperature / the same plant / the amount of iodine solution
scheme.examinerNote: Naming the independent variable again as the control earns nothing.

hints: Independent = what you chose to change. Dependent = what you measured. Control = what you deliberately kept the same.
parts.workedSolution: (i) whether that part of the leaf is covered by foil; (ii) the colour of that part when iodine solution is added, showing whether starch is present; (iii) the time the plant spends in the light, kept the same for every leaf.

The leaf removed after 10 hours had 74% of its area turning blue-black.
Complete the results table.

scheme.for: 74 written in the 10 hours row

hints: The unit is in the column heading, so the cell only needs the number.

parts.stem: Plot these results on the grid and draw a straight line of best fit.

scheme.for: axes labelled with quantity and unit as printed
scheme.examinerNote: Both axes are printed here, so the mark is for using the full grid sensibly.

scheme.for: all six points plotted correctly (within half a small square)
a straight line of best fit drawn
the anomalous point ignored when drawing the line

hints: Use a sharp HB pencil and a ruler; plot each point with a small cross or dot.
A line of best fit does not have to pass through every point, and it never zig-zags between them.
parts.workedSolution: Plot (0, 0), (2, 16), (4, 12), (6, 46), (8, 60) and (10, 74). Five of the six lie close to a straight line from the origin to (10, 74); the 4-hour point lies well below it, so leave it out and rule a single straight line through the rest.

commonErrors.feedback: Joining the points dot to dot loses the best-fit mark. Examiners in Summer 2024 and Summer 2025 reported this on both Booklet A and Booklet B: one ruled line through the trend, ignoring the anomaly.

parts.stem: Identify the anomalous result and suggest what the class should do about it.

accepted: the 4 hour result, and it should be repeated

any: ignore it when drawing the line
leave it out of the mean

scheme.for: the result at 4 hours (12%)
repeat that reading / leave it out when drawing the line of best fit

hints: The anomaly is the point that is far from the trend, not simply the smallest number.
parts.workedSolution: The 4-hour result, 12%, is anomalous: it is well below the line the other five points follow, and it is even lower than the 2-hour result. The class should repeat that leaf, and leave the point out when drawing the line of best fit.

commonErrors.feedback: An anomaly is left out of the mean and out of the line of best fit, and repeated if there is time. Keeping it drags the line away from the real trend.

parts.stem: Explain one change the class could make to improve the reliability of their results.

accepted: test more than one leaf at each time and compare the results

scheme.for: test several leaves at each time / repeat each reading
and compare them or calculate a mean, so an odd result shows up
scheme.examinerNote: Reliability is repeats and agreement; accuracy is closeness to the true value. Summer 2025 Booklet B reported the two being confused.

hints: Reliability is about repeating and comparing. Accuracy is about being close to the true value — a different question.
parts.workedSolution: Test three leaves at each time instead of one and compare the results, taking a mean. Repeats make an odd result obvious and show whether the pattern can be trusted.

commonErrors.feedback: Better equipment improves accuracy, not reliability. Reliability is improved by repeating the measurement and checking the repeats agree.

context.setting: A student asked to prove that chlorophyll is needed for photosynthesis

parts.stem:
A student has a variegated geranium, a dark cupboard and the usual laboratory apparatus.
Describe how she could show that chlorophyll is needed for photosynthesis.
Your written communication is assessed in this question, including your use of specialist scientific terms.

bands.descriptor: Five or six of the indicative points, described in detail, with specialist terms used widely and accurately; organised clearly; spelling, punctuation and grammar good enough that the meaning is clear throughout.
Three or four of the indicative points; some specialist vocabulary; organised with some clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar competent enough for the meaning to be clear.

indicativeContent.point: destarch the plant by leaving it in the dark for 48 hours
record or draw which parts of the chosen leaf are green and which are white
leave the plant in bright light for several hours, then remove the leaf
boil the leaf in water to kill it and break the cells open
boil it in ethanol with the Bunsen turned off to remove the chlorophyll
dip it in hot water to soften it, spread it on a white tile and add iodine solution
the green parts turn blue-black and the white parts stay yellow-brown, so chlorophyll is needed

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: A point contradicted elsewhere in the answer is not counted. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

hints: Order matters: destarch, record the pattern, light, then the four steps of the starch test, then the result.
Finish with the comparison — green went blue-black, white did not — or the conclusion point is not counted.
parts.workedSolution: Leave the plant for 48 hours in a dark cupboard to destarch it. Draw the chosen leaf, marking which parts are green and which are white. Put the plant in bright light for several hours, then remove that leaf. Boil it in water to kill it and break the cells open. Turn the Bunsen burner off and boil the leaf in ethanol standing in hot water, which removes the chlorophyll. Dip it in hot water to soften it, spread it on a white tile and add iodine solution. The parts that were green turn blue-black and the parts that were white stay yellow-brown, so starch was made only where chlorophyll was present.

commonErrors.feedback: Destarching is the first indicative point and the answer does not mention it. Without it the leaf could already contain starch and the result would prove nothing.

findTheMistake.stem: Cáit is asked to describe the starch test on a leaf. Her answer:
studentWorking: Take the leaf off the plant.
Put the leaf in a test tube of ethanol and heat it over a Bunsen burner until the ethanol boils.
Dip the leaf in hot water to soften it.
Spread the leaf on a white tile and add iodine solution.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Two things go wrong in one line. The leaf has not been boiled in water first, so it is still alive and its cell membranes are intact; and ethanol is being heated over a naked flame, which is the hazard the safety mark is about.
correction: Take the leaf off the plant.
Boil the leaf in water for about a minute to kill it and break the cells open.
Turn the Bunsen burner off. Stand a test tube of ethanol containing the leaf in a beaker of hot water until the chlorophyll has come out.
Dip the leaf in hot water to soften it, spread it on a white tile and add iodine solution.
findTheMistake.feedback: The last two steps are right and in order, so the softening and iodine points stand. The missing water bath costs the first point, and heating ethanol over a flame costs the safety point — Summer 2024 examiners were specific that the precaution here is switching the Bunsen off, not a general laboratory rule. Write the four steps as four sentences and the reasons follow naturally.

prompts.prompt: The four steps of the starch test, with a reason for each.
prompts.answer: 1 Boil in water — kills the leaf and breaks the cells open. 2 Boil in ethanol with the Bunsen off — removes the chlorophyll. 3 Dip in hot water — softens the brittle leaf. 4 Add iodine solution on a white tile — blue-black means starch.

prompts.prompt: How and why is a plant destarched?
prompts.answer: Leave it in the dark for 48 hours, so the starch already in the leaves is used up and any starch found afterwards must have been made during the investigation.

prompts.prompt: What is the safety precaution when a leaf is heated in ethanol, and why?
prompts.answer: Turn the Bunsen burner off and stand the tube in hot water, because ethanol is flammable.

prompts.prompt: Which solution absorbs carbon dioxide in a sealed flask, and which one releases it?
prompts.answer: Sodium hydroxide absorbs carbon dioxide. Sodium hydrogencarbonate releases it, which is how you give pondweed more.

prompts.prompt: What does a variegated leaf show, and which parts turn blue-black?
prompts.answer: That chlorophyll is needed for photosynthesis. Only the green parts turn blue-black; the white parts have no chlorophyll and stay yellow-brown.

prompts.prompt: What is the test for oxygen and its result?
prompts.answer: Put a glowing splint into the gas: it relights.

prompts.prompt: Reliability or accuracy — which is improved by repeating a reading?
prompts.answer: Reliability. Repeats that agree show the result can be trusted. Accuracy is how close a measurement is to the true value, and is improved by better technique or a better instrument.
